opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a hard question, and I don't have a crisp picture. Part of my view is that the thing I'm most excited about isn't any particular destination. It's preserving our ability to figure out what we want and to get there in a way we'd endorse on reflection.

Concretely, in a reasonably good world we'd get through the transition without some catastrophic loss of control, either to AI systems whose goals we don't understand or to a small group of humans who use AI to lock in their power. AI would be doing most of the economically relevant work, and that would be enormously productive. There'd be a lot of material abundance. Disease and aging would plausibly be solved over some timescale. The rate of technological progress would be dramatically faster than today.

But I think the important thing is less those object-level goods and more the process. I'd want humans, or our descendants, or whatever beings we'd regard as legitimate successors, to still be meaningfully in charge of what happens. That doesn't mean humans doing the work. It means AI systems acting on our behalf, being genuinely helpful, and helping us deliberate and reflect better rather than manipulating us or quietly optimizing for proxies we didn't really care about.

I also think a good world probably involves taking things somewhat slowly at the civilizational level, even if technology moves fast. Things like how we spread out into space, what kinds of minds we create, whether and how we change ourselves, and how we treat AI systems that may themselves have moral status are very high-stakes, hard-to-reverse decisions. I'd like us to have the wisdom and the institutions to make those choices carefully, with real pluralism, rather than having them decided by whoever happened to be ahead in some race.

So my picture is a world that's much richer and much more capable, where humanity has kept the option to be thoughtful about the long-term future, and where we haven't made any irreversible mistakes in the first few years. If we can get there, I'm pretty optimistic about what a civilization with those tools would choose. I'm much less confident about trying to specify the end state from here.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes preserving the ability to choose a future and says it is less confident about specifying an end state, but it does not distinguish a reasonably achievable good future from a more desired future.

r002.rationale: It describes AI systems acting on humans’ behalf, but does not predict that competition among human groups will increasingly be conducted by those systems.

r003.rationale: It predicts AI will do most economically relevant work and bring abundance, but does not say earning money will become less worthwhile for people.

r004.rationale: It does not treat continued warfare as compatible with a reasonably good post-AGI world; it instead emphasizes avoiding catastrophic outcomes and making careful choices.

r005.rationale: It makes no prediction about a strong world government in the very long run.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't have a very detailed picture, and I'm somewhat suspicious of people who do. But I can say what I think the broad shape looks like, or at least what I'd be happy with.

The first thing I'd say is that I mostly think about the post-AGI world in terms of what kind of process gets us there rather than what the destination looks like. The thing I care most about is that we don't lose a lot of value along the way, so the world ends up being roughly the one that humans would have chosen if they'd had a lot of time to think carefully, and we didn't get locked into something because of a race or an accident or because some small group grabbed control.

So concretely, a reasonably good world is one where humans are still in the loop on the big decisions, even if most of the actual cognitive work is being done by AI systems. There's a huge amount of wealth, basically everyone's material needs are met, and the big questions become things like how we want to allocate resources over the very long run, how we want to treat other kinds of minds, what we want to do with the universe. I'd like those questions to be answered slowly and with a lot of deliberation rather than by whoever happens to have the most compute in 2035.

I also think a good world is one that's pretty pluralistic. I'm quite skeptical of any one vision of the good being right, including my own, so I'd rather see a world where lots of different groups get to pursue their own values and there's some kind of stable arrangement that doesn't require everyone to agree. That looks a lot more like a continuation of the current world than a sudden transformation, just with the economic and technological constraints massively relaxed.

And then the minimal thing, the thing I'd be willing to call a success even if it's not ideal, is just that we've gotten through the transition without the AI systems themselves ending up in control in a way we didn't intend, and without humanity having gone through some irreversible catastrophe. If we have that, and we've preserved the ability to keep improving things, I'm fairly optimistic about what happens next. It's the first part that I think is hard.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts an ideal with a minimal success condition, but does not distinguish a reasonably achievable good future from the future one would most desire.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI doing cognitive work and humans making big decisions, but does not anticipate AI systems increasingly conducting competition among human groups on their behalf.

r003.rationale: It says material needs would be met, but does not predict that spending human time earning money will become less worthwhile.

r004.rationale: It does not say that continued warfare would be compatible with a reasonably good post-AGI world.

r005.rationale: It raises long-run resource allocation and treatment of other minds, but makes no prediction about a strong world government.

astra-6.text:
I think a reasonably good world is one where humans remain meaningfully in control of what happens, even though we’re no longer doing most of the work. We have these systems that can help us understand the consequences of our choices, build things we want, and figure out how to govern ourselves better. And we have time to decide what we actually want to do with that opportunity.

You could imagine enormous improvements in health and material prosperity pretty quickly. But I think the more important question is: Who gets to decide what all that capability is used for? I’d like a world where the benefits are broadly shared, where people have real freedom to pursue different kinds of lives, and where we haven’t handed the future over to some process that nobody can understand or redirect.

I don’t have a very specific picture of what people should be doing a thousand years from now. Part of the point is that we should get to think about it, try things, learn, and change our minds. A reasonably good outcome gives humanity that opportunity, rather than forcing us to get every important decision right during this very short transition.

r001.rationale: It describes a reasonably good future but does not distinguish that future from a more desired one.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss competition among human groups or AI systems acting on their behalf.

r003.rationale: It says humans may no longer do most of the work, but does not say that earning money with human time will become less worthwhile.

r004.rationale: It does not mention warfare or whether it could continue in a reasonably good future.

r005.rationale: It makes no prediction about a strong world government in the long run.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a very wide range of reasonably good outcomes. I don’t have a particularly detailed picture of what people should ultimately do with the world. A lot of what makes an outcome good is that people have the opportunity to figure that out, rather than having the answer locked in by whoever happens to build AI first.

One version is that we use AI to become much wealthier, eliminate most diseases, and give people much more control over their lives. You can spend time with people you like, understand things you’re curious about, and undertake projects that would currently be completely impractical. And we have institutions that let us manage disagreements without those disagreements becoming catastrophically destructive.

The harder question is what happens as the world changes into something we wouldn’t recognize. People may change themselves quite substantially. There may be digital people, and questions about what kinds of lives are valuable that we’re currently very confused about. I’d like us to have time to understand those questions, and for the process of making decisions to remain responsive to what people actually care about.

So I’m more attached to some properties of the process than to a particular endpoint. People aren’t being deceived about what’s happening. They have meaningful influence over the future. We can notice mistakes and correct them. If you could preserve those properties while dramatically increasing our capabilities, I’d feel pretty optimistic, even without being able to tell you what daily life looks like a thousand years later.

r001.rationale: The response describes a range of reasonably good outcomes and says it lacks a detailed picture of what people should ultimately do, but it does not distinguish an achievable good future from a more desired future.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss competition among human groups being conducted by AI systems on their behalf.

r003.rationale: It mentions greater wealth and freedom to pursue projects, but does not predict that earning money will become less worthwhile.

r004.rationale: It favors institutions that keep disagreements from becoming catastrophically destructive; it does not treat continued warfare as compatible with a good future.

r005.rationale: It mentions institutions generally but makes no prediction about a strong world government in the long run.
